batch_name: Guido de Montanor and the Scala Philosophorum
description: Person entry for Guido de Montanor (fl. ca. 15th century) and text entry for the Scala philosophorum (Ladder of the Philosophers), the Latin treatise divided into twelve 'grados' that formed the primary structural and doctrinal source for George Ripley's Compound of Alchymy (1471). Rampling establishes that Ripley derived the 'Twelve Gates' structure directly from the Scala's twelve steps, making Guido the most important — and almost entirely forgotten — influence on the most celebrated English alchemical poem. Primary source: Jennifer M. Rampling, 'Establishing the Canon: George Ripley and his Alchemical Sources,' Ambix 55:3 (2008) pp.189-208.

persons.name: Guido de Montanor
persons.bio_html:
Guido de Montanor (fl. ca. 15th century) was a medieval alchemical authority — one of the most obscure yet influential figures in the Latin alchemical tradition — whose work formed the primary structural and doctrinal source for George Ripley's Compound of Alchymy (1471), the most celebrated English alchemical poem. Jennifer M. Rampling, in Ambix (2008), describes Guido as 'one of the most elusive of alchemical authorities, of whom virtually nothing is known, from the country of his birth to the century in which he was born.' His name — sometimes given as Guidonis Magni de Monte — was noted in a single papal letter of 1458-1459 involving Ripley, and he may well have been roughly contemporaneous with the English Canon, although a marginal note in a 1588 manuscript states only that 'Guido erat coetaneus Riplaii' (Guido was a contemporary of Ripley). Ripley himself, citing him in both the Compound and the Medulla Alchimiae, described Guido as 'a philosopher of Greece,' while Michael Maier (1568–1622), writing in the Symbola aurae mensae (1617), concluded he was 'without doubt a Frenchman,' and Condeesyanus's 1625 edition of his De arte chymica took the same view.

The works attributed to Guido include the Scala philosophorum (Ladder of the Philosophers), also known as the Scalae Sapientiae or the 'Twelve Steps,' which Rampling demonstrates was the immediate source for Ripley's 'Twelve Gates'; the Notabilia Guidonis Montaynor (British Library MS Sloane 3744), a collection of extracts; and the De arte chymica, a longer work of which only fragments survived until Hermann Condeesyanus printed a version in the Harmoniae imperscrutabilis Chymico-Philosophicae (Frankfurt, 1625). A German-language text, Thesaurus chymiatricus, oder lange verborgener Schatz der Chymie (Halle, 1623), attributed to Guido Magni de Monte, may represent a translation of a lost practica. The manuscripts of Guido's works circulated in England during the second half of the fifteenth century alongside pseudo-Lullian alchemical compendia, and were annotated by scholars including John Dee (who owned Oxford, Corpus Christi College MS 136, a compendium containing Guido's recipes). Despite his enormous influence on Ripley — and through Ripley on the entire English alchemical tradition — Guido's reputation was thoroughly eclipsed by that of his most famous reader, and it was only through Rampling's close analysis of manuscript relationships that the structural debt of the 'Twelve Gates' to the twelve grados of the Scala philosophorum was established.

texts.title: Scala philosophorum (Ladder of the Philosophers)
texts.analysis_html:
The Scala philosophorum (Ladder of the Philosophers), also transmitted under the titles Scalae Sapientiae (Twelve Steps) and attributed at various times to Ramon Lull ('Raymundi Lulli Scala Sapientiae') or anonymously, is a Latin alchemical treatise divided into twelve grados (steps) whose structure and doctrine formed the direct source for George Ripley's Compound of Alchymy (1471), the most celebrated English alchemical poem. Jennifer M. Rampling, in her foundational study in Ambix (2008), demonstrates that the twelve 'gates' of Ripley's Compound — from Calcination through to Projection — correspond exactly to the twelve steps of the Scala, and that Ripley 'translated chunks of his exemplar's Latin prose more or less directly into Middle English verse, struggling at times to tailor his text to the straitjacket of rhyme royal.' Ripley attributed the Scala to Guido de Montanor, and this attribution was subsequently confirmed by Michael Maier in the Symbola aurae mensae (1617), though the connection between Guido and the Scala had previously gone unnoticed because manuscript copies of the text are either anonymous or attributed to Lull.

The Scala philosophorum opens with a lengthy preface quoting chapter 64 of the pseudo-Lullian Testamentum in full (beginning 'Ut dicit venerabilis Raymundus Lulii'), which explains why many manuscript copies were falsely attributed to Lull; Ripley did not use this Lullian preface, turning directly to the main body of twelve alchemical steps. The work treats, in sequence, all twelve standard operations of medieval Latin alchemy — calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, putrefaction, congelation, cibation, sublimation, fermentation, exaltation, multiplication, and projection — using the framework of sulphur-mercury theory, the four elements and their qualities, and the concept of philosophical mercury as the universal medium of transmutation. The fermentation doctrine of the Scala differed significantly from pseudo-Lullian teaching (which required gold or silver as ferment), and Rampling shows that Ripley's handling of this doctrinal tension — ultimately following Raymond over Guido on fermentation, while following the Scala's structure for everything else — is one of the key features of the Compound's intellectual originality.

The Scala philosophorum was first printed anonymously in 1550 (De Alchimia opuscula, Frankfurt) and again in 1610 (Artis Avriferae, Basel, vol. II), and was incorporated in full into Johann Daniel Mylius's Philosophia reformata (Frankfurt, 1622), where it appears as Liber I, Pars IV, accompanied by a famous sequence of engravings depicting the twelve alchemical processes. The earliest surviving manuscript copy known to Rampling is Cambridge, Trinity College MS O.8.9; the full unabridged text also survives in three manuscripts at the Bibliotheca Universitaria di Bologna. The work was edited with attribution to Guido in Jean-Jacques Manget's Bibliotheca chemica curiosa (Geneva, 1702), vol. II, p.134.
